readings.title: The Little Black Boy (Songs of Innocence)
readings.challenge: Follow a story told inside a story: a boy repeats his mother’s words, then adds his own.
readings.focus: A child uses his mother’s comfort to imagine a day when he and an English boy are equal before God.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Innocence. Blake wrote it while British ships still carried enslaved Africans across the ocean and people argued about ending slavery. The speaker is a Black child born in Africa, “the southern wild.” Bereaved means robbed of something loved.
readings.contentNote: The speaker uses the ideas of Blake’s time that joined whiteness with goodness and darkness with the lack of light (“my soul is white”; “as if bereaved of light”). Many readers think Blake set down those ideas in order to question them; they are the poem’s historical language, not the site’s view, and are worth talking about openly.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Innocence, “The Little Black Boy,” the complete poem; opens “My mother bore me in the southern wild, And I am black, but O my soul is white! White as…”; closes “…then I’ll stand and stroke his silver hair, And be like him, and he will then love me.”.

questions.prompt: Where did the boy’s mother teach him, and which way did she point?
facilitatorNotes: Under a tree, before the heat of the day, pointing East toward the rising sun. Everything she teaches grows from that sunrise.
evidence: My mother taught me underneath a tree,
And, pointing to the East, began to say:

questions.prompt: What does the mother say the sun gives away, and who receives it?
facilitatorNotes: Light and heat; flowers, trees, beasts and men all receive comfort and joy from it. She describes a gift shared by every living thing, not only some.
evidence: And gives His light, and gives His heat away,
And flowers and trees and beasts and men receive

questions.prompt: The mother calls their dark skin “a cloud” and “a shady grove.” What does she believe will happen to the cloud one day?
facilitatorNotes: It will vanish when their souls have learned to bear the heat of God’s love, and God will call them out to rejoice. In her picture a body is like a cloud over the soul. Notice that the boy later gives the English child a “white cloud” too: everyone has one.
evidence: Are but a cloud, and like a shady grove.
The cloud will vanish, we shall hear His voice,

questions.prompt: At the end the boy plans to shade the English boy “till he can bear” the heat, and hopes “he will then love me.” What does that hope tell you about the boy now? What do you think of his plan?
facilitatorNotes: He is the stronger and kinder one in his own picture, yet he still has to hope for love, which suggests he does not have it now. Some readers hear generosity in the ending; others hear sadness and unfairness, because the Black child must earn a love the English child is simply given. Both readings use the text.
evidence: I’ll shade him from the heat till he can bear
And be like him, and he will then love me.

readings.title: The Chimney-Sweeper (Songs of Innocence)
readings.challenge: Hear one word with two meanings, and decide whether the speaker believes his own ending.
readings.focus: A small sweep comforts his friend, and a dream offers the freedom that daytime does not.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Innocence. In Blake’s London, boys as young as four or five were sold or bound to master sweeps and sent up inside narrow chimneys to brush out soot, the black dust left by coal fires. They walked the streets calling “Sweep!”
readings.contentNote: A mother dies and a father sells his young son into hard, dangerous work. In a dream, children lie locked in coffins until an angel frees them.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Innocence, “The Chimney-Sweeper,” the complete poem; opens “When my mother died I was very young, And my father sold me while yet my tongue Could…”; closes “…was cold, Tom was happy and warm: So, if all do their duty, they need not fear harm.”.

questions.prompt: The boy could “scarcely cry” the sweep’s street call. What comes out instead, and what two meanings can you hear in it?
facilitatorNotes: He is too young to say “sweep” clearly, so it comes out “weep”: his street call and the sound of crying at once.
evidence: Could scarcely cry ‘Weep! weep! weep! weep!’

questions.prompt: How does the speaker comfort Tom Dacre when his curly hair is shaved?
facilitatorNotes: He says that now the soot cannot spoil his white hair. It is a strange comfort, since there is no hair left to spoil; ask whether it would comfort them.
evidence: ‘Hush, Tom! never mind it, for, when your head’s bare,
You know that the soot cannot spoil your white hair.’

questions.prompt: Compare the sweepers in Tom’s dream before and after the angel comes.
facilitatorNotes: Before, they are locked in black coffins; after, they leap and laugh down a green plain, wash in a river, shine in the sun, and leave their bags behind. Darkness, soot and stillness change to light, water and play.
evidence: Were all of them locked up in coffins of black.
And wash in a river, and shine in the sun.

questions.prompt: The poem ends, “So, if all do their duty, they need not fear harm.” Does the rest of the poem make you believe that lesson?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker seems to believe it, and Tom wakes happy. But the boys rise in the dark, the morning is cold, and the people who sold them are never blamed. Many readers think Blake wants us to doubt a lesson the child has been taught; others hear real comfort. Ask for a line on each side.
evidence: Though the morning was cold, Tom was happy and warm:
So, if all do their duty, they need not fear harm.

readings.title: The Little Boy Lost and The Little Boy Found (Songs of Innocence)
readings.challenge: Read two short poems as one story with a gap in the middle, and say what happens in the gap.
readings.focus: A child lost in the dark is frightened, then found and brought home.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. These two poems are from Songs of Innocence, printed one after the other. A fen is a marsh; mire is deep mud; vapour is mist. The “wandering light” is a will-o’-the-wisp, a flickering light seen over marshes at night, which old stories said led travellers astray. Nigh means near; a dale is a valley.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Innocence, “The Little Boy Lost” and “The Little Boy Found,” both complete poems; opens “‘Father, father, where are you going? O do not walk so fast! Speak, father, speak to your…”; closes “…brought, Who in sorrow pale, through the lonely dale, Her little boy weeping sought.”.

questions.prompt: What does the boy beg his father to do in the first stanza? What has happened by the second?
facilitatorNotes: He asks his father to slow down and speak to him. Then “no father was there”: the boy is alone, wet with dew, crying in deep mud, and the mist flies away. Some readers think the “father” he was following was the misty light all along.
evidence: O do not walk so fast!
The night was dark, no father was there,

questions.prompt: In the second poem, what leads the boy, and who appears to him?
facilitatorNotes: The “wandering light” leads him deeper into the marsh. When he cries, God appears “like his father, in white,” kisses him and leads him by the hand.
evidence: Led by the wandering light,
Appeared like his father, in white.

questions.prompt: Who has been searching for the boy, and how does Blake show her feelings?
facilitatorNotes: His mother, “in sorrow pale,” weeping as she searched through the lonely valley. We see her only at the end, so readers learn that someone at home was frightened too.
evidence: Who in sorrow pale, through the lonely dale,
Her little boy weeping sought.

questions.prompt: Blake made this one story into two poems. Why might he leave the boy alone and crying at the end of the first one?
facilitatorNotes: The break makes readers feel the child’s fear before the comfort comes, the way a frightened child cannot know rescue is near. Others may say the two poems answer each other, like many pairs in Blake’s songs. Either view should point to how each poem ends.
evidence: The child was wet with dew;
And to his mother brought,

readings.title: Night (Songs of Innocence)
readings.challenge: Keep track of who is speaking when the poem’s last two stanzas give a voice to a lion.
readings.focus: Night is watched over by unseen angels, and a fierce animal is imagined made gentle.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Innocence. As night falls, Blake imagines angels moving unseen among sleeping animals and people. A fold is a fenced pen that keeps sheep safe at night; wrath is fierce anger; meekness is gentleness.
readings.contentNote: Wolves and tigers hunt sheep, and the poem says the angels receive the spirits of those that are killed.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Innocence, “Night,” the complete poem; opens “The sun descending in the West, The evening star does shine; The birds are silent in…”; closes “…river, My bright mane for ever Shall shine like the gold, As I guard o’er the fold.’”.

questions.prompt: Find three signs of evening in the first stanza.
facilitatorNotes: The sun goes down in the West, the evening star shines, the birds are silent, and the moon “sits and smiles.”
evidence: The sun descending in the West,
The birds are silent in their nest,

questions.prompt: What do the angels do when they find someone weeping who should be asleep?
facilitatorNotes: They pour sleep on the weeper’s head and sit down by the bed, as a parent might.
evidence: They pour sleep on their head,
And sit down by their bed.

questions.prompt: The angels cannot always stop the wolves and tigers. What does the poem say happens then?
facilitatorNotes: They weep and try to drive the hunger away; if the beasts rush in anyway, the angels receive each “mild spirit” into new worlds. Blake does not pretend the danger is gone; the comfort is what comes after.
evidence: But, if they rush dreadful,
Receive each mild spirit,

questions.prompt: In the last two stanzas the lion speaks. How has he changed, and why might Blake end the poem with him?
facilitatorNotes: The lion weeps golden tears, lies down beside the lamb and guards the fold he once threatened. Ending with him shows the poem’s biggest hope: that fierceness itself can turn gentle. Some readers notice this happens in “our immortal day,” another world, not this one.
evidence: I can lie down and sleep,
As I guard o’er the fold.’

readings.title: On Another’s Sorrow (Songs of Innocence)
readings.challenge: Answer a chain of questions that all expect the same answer, and notice how the chain grows.
readings.focus: If people cannot see sorrow without sharing it, the poem argues, God cannot either.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Innocence. It speaks from Christian belief: the God who “becomes an infant small” is Jesus. Those are the poem’s beliefs, which readers may or may not share. Woe means great sadness.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Innocence, “On Another’s Sorrow,” the complete poem; opens “Can I see another’s woe, And not be in sorrow too? Can I see another’s grief, And not…”; closes “…our grief He may destroy: Till our grief is fled and gone He doth sit by us and moan.”.

questions.prompt: What answer does the speaker give to the poem’s questions? How many times does he give it?
facilitatorNotes: “No, no! never can it be!” and then “O no! never can it be!”, each followed by “Never, never can it be!”: twice, at the end of the third and sixth stanzas.
evidence: No, no! never can it be!
O no! never can it be!

questions.prompt: Find the small creature whose sorrows the poem mentions. Why might Blake choose such a small one?
facilitatorNotes: The wren, with “sorrows small.” If the smallest bird’s grief is noticed, then no grief is too small to matter.
evidence: Hear the wren with sorrows small,

questions.prompt: The first three stanzas ask about “I,” a father and a mother. How do they prepare for the questions about God?
facilitatorNotes: They show that ordinary people cannot watch someone suffer without suffering too; then the poem asks the same about God. It argues from what we know to what we cannot see.
evidence: Can I see another’s woe,
And can He who smiles on all

questions.prompt: The poem ends with Him who “doth sit by us and moan.” Is that a comforting ending or a sad one?
facilitatorNotes: The comfort is company rather than a quick fix: someone grieves beside you until the grief is gone. Some readers find “moan” sad; others find it the kindest word in the poem. Either view can be supported.
evidence: Till our grief is fled and gone
He doth sit by us and moan.

readings.title: The Clod and the Pebble (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Compare two songs that use almost the same words to say opposite things.
readings.focus: Two small things answer the question “What is love?” and Blake leaves readers to judge.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. A clod is a lump of earth; “metres meet” means fitting verses; “in heaven’s despite” means in spite of heaven.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Clod and the Pebble,” the complete poem; opens “‘Love seeketh not itself to please, Nor for itself hath any care, But for another gives…”; closes “…to its delight, Joys in another’s loss of ease, And builds a hell in heaven’s despite.’”.

questions.prompt: Where is each singer? What has happened to the clod?
facilitatorNotes: The clod lies where cattle have trodden on it; the pebble lies in a brook.
evidence: Trodden with the cattle’s feet,
But a pebble of the brook

questions.prompt: Compare the first line of each song. Which words stay the same, and which change?
facilitatorNotes: “Love seeketh … to please” stays; “not itself” becomes “only Self.” The last lines swap too: a heaven built in hell becomes a hell built in heaven. A tiny change of words turns the meaning around.
evidence: Love seeketh not itself to please,
Love seeketh only Self to please,

questions.prompt: Why might a soft clod sing about giving, and a hard, smooth pebble sing about getting?
facilitatorNotes: The clod gives way under every foot; the pebble stays hard while the water runs over it. Each song fits its singer. Some readers say the clod has learned love by suffering; others think it simply cannot help being stepped on.
evidence: So sung a little clod of clay,
Warbled out these metres meet:

questions.prompt: Blake never says which singer is right. Which song describes love better, in your view? Could both be true?
facilitatorNotes: No single answer is expected. Many readers think both kinds of love are real; the pebble’s love wants “to bind another,” which sounds like owning someone. Ask for an example from a story or from life.
evidence: But for another gives its ease,
To bind another to its delight,

readings.title: Holy Thursday (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Notice when a poet describes weather that is not really weather.
readings.focus: A rich country lets its children go hungry, and the speaker refuses to call that holy.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. Once a year thousands of poor children from London’s charity schools were marched into St Paul’s Cathedral to sing; Blake’s “Holy Thursday” in Songs of Innocence describes that service. This poem looks at the same children again. A usurous hand gives only to get back more; to appal is to horrify.
readings.contentNote: The poem is about children going hungry in a wealthy country.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “Holy Thursday,” the complete poem; opens “Is this a holy thing to see In a rich and fruitful land,— Babes reduced to misery, Fed…”; closes “…And where’er the rain does fall, Babe can never hunger there, Nor poverty the mind appal.”.

questions.prompt: What question opens the poem? What kind of land does the speaker finally say it is?
facilitatorNotes: Whether it is holy to see babies in misery in a rich land; he answers that it is “a land of poverty,” though it is rich and fruitful.
evidence: In a rich and fruitful land,—
It is a land of poverty!

questions.prompt: The children are singing. What does the speaker hear instead of a song?
facilitatorNotes: A “trembling cry.” He doubts that it can be a song of joy when so many children are poor.
evidence: Is that trembling cry a song?
Can it be a song of joy?

questions.prompt: “It is eternal winter there.” Is the speaker describing real weather? What could the winter stand for?
facilitatorNotes: No: the land is fruitful. The sunless days, bare fields and thorny paths stand for the children’s hard, uncared-for lives. Some readers see cold hearts as well as cold lives.
evidence: And their fields are bleak and bare,
It is eternal winter there.

questions.prompt: Why does the last stanza say that where the sun shines and the rain falls, no baby can go hungry?
facilitatorNotes: The land has plenty of both, so hunger there cannot be blamed on nature: it must be people who let it happen. The ending turns a picture into an accusation.
evidence: For where’er the sun does shine,
Babe can never hunger there,

readings.title: The Little Girl Lost and Found, part 1: The Little Girl Lost (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Follow a poem that begins with a prophecy and then tells a strange story about wild beasts.
readings.focus: A lost girl falls asleep in the desert, and the beasts of prey treat her gently.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. It has a second part, “The Little Girl Found,” which follows it. Futurity means the future; to prophesy is to tell what will happen; “grave the sentence deep” means carve these words deep, so they are remembered. A clime is a land; its “prime” is its best season. Beasts of prey hunt other animals; gambolled means leaped about playfully; hallowed means holy; conveyed means carried.
readings.contentNote: A seven-year-old girl is lost in the desert and carried off by lions while she sleeps; she is not hurt.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Little Girl Lost,” the first of two linked poems, complete; opens “In futurity I prophesy That the earth from sleep (Grave the sentence deep)”; closes “…the lioness Loosed her slender dress, And naked they conveyed To caves the sleeping maid.”.

questions.prompt: The poem opens with a prophecy. What does the speaker say will happen one day?
facilitatorNotes: The earth will wake from sleep and look for its Maker, and the wild desert will become a gentle garden. Keep this in mind: the story that follows may be a small picture of it.
evidence: That the earth from sleep
And the desert wild Become a garden mild.

questions.prompt: Why can’t Lyca fall asleep at first? What does she decide?
facilitatorNotes: She worries that her mother is weeping for her: “How can Lyca sleep If her mother weep?” She decides that if her mother’s heart aches she will stay awake, and if her mother sleeps she will not cry. She thinks of her mother before herself.
evidence: How can Lyca sleep If her mother weep?
If my mother sleep, Lyca shall not weep.

questions.prompt: What do the beasts of prey do when they find Lyca asleep?
facilitatorNotes: The lion gambols round her, bows his golden mane, licks her and weeps “ruby tears”; leopards and tigers play; the lioness loosens her dress and they carry her to their caves. Ask readers which detail is most surprising for a lion.
evidence: Then he gambolled round O’er the hallowed ground.
Ruby tears there came;

questions.prompt: Lions and tigers are dangerous. Why might Blake make them gentle in this poem?
facilitatorNotes: One answer links back to the prophecy: in the world to come, the wild desert becomes “a garden mild,” and even beasts of prey are kind. Others may think the animals sense that Lyca is innocent, or that the whole scene is like a dream. Readers should connect their answer to a line.
evidence: While the beasts of prey,
Bowed his mane of gold,

readings.title: The Little Girl Lost and Found, part 2: The Little Girl Found (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Compare what the parents fear with what they find.
readings.focus: A terrifying lion turns out to be a guide, and fear gives way to wonder.
readings.context: Recap: in “The Little Girl Lost,” seven-year-old Lyca wandered into the desert, worried that her mother was weeping, and fell asleep; lions, leopards and tigers played round her gently, and the lions carried her to their caves. Woe-begone means full of sorrow; “making moan” means crying out in grief; a “fancied image” is something imagined; famished means starving. A couching lion is lying low, ready to spring. A dell is a small wooded valley.
readings.contentNote: The parents dream that their child is starving and dying; a lion knocks them to the ground.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Little Girl Found,” the second of two linked poems, complete; opens “All the night in woe Lyca’s parents go Over valleys deep, While the deserts weep.”; closes “To this day they dwell In a lonely dell, Nor fear the wolvish howl Nor the lion’s growl.”.

questions.prompt: How long do Lyca’s parents search, and what do they dream at night?
facilitatorNotes: Seven days and seven nights. They dream they see their child starving in the desert, weak and shrieking. The poem stays with their fear for many stanzas.
evidence: Arm in arm, seven days
And dream they see their child Starved in desert wild.

questions.prompt: What does the lion do when he meets the parents? When do their fears go away?
facilitatorNotes: He knocks them to the ground and walks round them, sniffing, as if they are prey. Their fears ease when he licks their hands and stands silently beside them; then they see he is a spirit with a crown and golden hair.
evidence: Smelling to his prey;
When he licks their hands,

questions.prompt: What does the lion tell them, and what do they find when they follow him?
facilitatorNotes: Not to weep: Lyca is asleep in his palace. They find her sleeping “Among tigers wild,” safe.
evidence: Weep not for the maid;
And saw their sleeping child Among tigers wild.

questions.prompt: The parents imagined their child starving, but found her safe. What does the poem suggest about fear? Do you agree with how it ends?
facilitatorNotes: What they feared was a “fancied image”; the real lion was gentle and the danger was in their minds. Some readers find the ending comforting; others find it strange that the family stays in the wild for ever. Both are fair readings of the last stanza.
evidence: The fancied image strays,
Nor fear the wolvish howl

readings.title: The Chimney-Sweeper (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Find where the child’s own words begin, and follow his reasons to the end.
readings.focus: A small sweep explains why being cheerful does not mean he has not been harmed.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. Sweeps were small boys sent up inside chimneys to brush out soot; they called “Sweep!” in the streets, which a young child might pronounce “’weep.” A heath is open, wild land.
readings.contentNote: A small child works in the snow while his parents are at church; he blames them, and the church and king they praise, for his misery.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Chimney-Sweeper,” the complete poem; opens “A little black thing among the snow, Crying! ‘weep! weep!’ in notes of woe! ‘Where are…”; closes “…And are gone to praise God and His priest and king, Who made up a heaven of our misery.’”.

questions.prompt: Who asks the question in the third line, and who answers? Where do the child’s words begin and end?
facilitatorNotes: Someone passing asks where his parents are; the child answers from “They are both gone up” to the end of the poem. The quotation marks show it.
evidence: ‘Where are thy father and mother? Say!’—

questions.prompt: What are “the clothes of death” the child was dressed in?
facilitatorNotes: The sweep’s black, sooty clothes. The work was dangerous and could kill a child, so his work clothes are also death’s clothes.
evidence: They clothed me in the clothes of death,

questions.prompt: The child still dances and sings. What do his parents think that proves? Does he agree?
facilitatorNotes: They think it proves they have done him no injury. He does not agree: being cheerful is just how he was before, on the heath, and it hides the harm.
evidence: And because I am happy and dance and sing,
They think they have done me no injury,

questions.prompt: Why might Blake put “God and His priest and king” in the same stanza as “our misery”?
facilitatorNotes: The child says the people his parents praise “made up a heaven” out of children’s suffering: they talk of heaven while children work. Some readers hear him blaming the church and king; others think he blames the parents for praising them. Both readings fit the line.
evidence: And are gone to praise God and His priest and king,
Who made up a heaven of our misery.’

readings.title: Nurse’s Song (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Read a very short poem twice, and decide how its speaker feels.
readings.focus: A grown-up watches children play and feels something that is not joy.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. A nurse here is a woman who looks after children. Songs of Innocence has a “Nurse’s Song” that begins almost the same way, in which the nurse lets the children play until dark. A dale is a valley; “in disguise” means hiding what is really felt.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “Nurse’s Song,” the complete poem; opens “When the voices of children are heard on the green, And whisperings are in the dale, The…”; closes “…Your spring and your day are wasted in play, And your winter and night in disguise.”.

questions.prompt: What does the nurse hear, and what does it make her remember?
facilitatorNotes: Children’s voices on the green and whispering in the valley; they bring back the days of her own youth.
evidence: When the voices of children are heard on the green,
The days of my youth rise fresh in my mind,

questions.prompt: “My face turns green and pale.” What feeling might turn a face green? Why might the nurse feel it?
facilitatorNotes: Envy, jealousy or sickness. She may envy the children’s freedom or regret her own lost youth; readers may also suggest worry.
evidence: My face turns green and pale.

questions.prompt: What does she say the children are wasting? Do you agree that play is wasted time?
facilitatorNotes: Their spring and their day: their youth. Readers may well disagree with her, and Blake may want them to.
evidence: Your spring and your day are wasted in play,

questions.prompt: What might “your winter and night in disguise” mean for the children’s lives?
facilitatorNotes: Winter and night may be grown-up life, which she expects them to spend hiding their real feelings. It is a hard line; accept careful guesses that use the seasons.
evidence: And your winter and night in disguise.

readings.title: The Sick Rose (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Reread a very short poem slowly and notice how much each word carries.
readings.focus: Something hidden and secret harms something beautiful.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. It is only eight lines long, so read it two or three times. Crimson is deep red. Gardeners know that tiny grubs and insects can eat a flower from the inside, where no one sees them.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Sick Rose,” the complete poem; opens “O rose, thou art sick! The invisible worm, That flies in the night, In the howling storm,”; closes “Has found out thy bed Of crimson joy, And his dark secret love Does thy life destroy.”.

questions.prompt: Who is the speaker talking to? What is the first thing they say?
facilitatorNotes: To the rose itself, as if it could hear: “O rose, thou art sick!” Speaking straight to a flower makes the poem feel like a warning or a sad discovery.
evidence: O rose, thou art sick!

questions.prompt: What has the worm done, and when does it come?
facilitatorNotes: It has found the rose’s bed and is destroying its life. It comes at night, flying in a howling storm.
evidence: That flies in the night,
Has found out thy bed

questions.prompt: Which words make the worm seem sneaky or frightening?
facilitatorNotes: “Invisible,” “night,” “howling storm,” and “dark secret.” The rose cannot see it coming. Readers may also notice that a worm that “flies” is no ordinary earthworm.
evidence: The invisible worm,
And his dark secret love

questions.prompt: Blake calls the worm’s feeling “love,” but it destroys the rose. How can love do harm? What else might this poem be about besides a flower?
facilitatorNotes: The worm wants the rose for itself and eats it from inside. Some readers think of anything hidden that spoils something lovely, such as a secret, a sickness or a jealous friendship; others keep to the garden. Ask for a line that supports each idea.
evidence: Of crimson joy,
Does thy life destroy.

readings.title: The Fly (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Read very short lines slowly enough to follow one long thought.
readings.focus: A small careless act makes the speaker wonder whether he is any different from a fly.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. The speaker has just brushed a fly away without thinking.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Fly,” the complete poem; opens “Little Fly, Thy summer’s play My thoughtless hand Has brushed away.”; closes “Then am I A happy fly. If I live, Or if I die.”.

questions.prompt: What has the speaker done to the fly, and how did it happen?
facilitatorNotes: His “thoughtless hand” brushed away the fly’s summer play: he did not mean it or even think about it.
evidence: My thoughtless hand
Has brushed away.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker say he is like a fly? Find what he does.
facilitatorNotes: He dances, drinks and sings until some “blind hand” brushes his wing: his life could end just as suddenly.
evidence: For I dance,
Shall brush my wing.

questions.prompt: Who or what might the “blind hand” be?
facilitatorNotes: Death, chance, fate or God are all possible. The word “blind” matters: the hand does not see what it does, just as his own hand was “thoughtless.”
evidence: Till some blind hand

questions.prompt: The poem says that “thought is life.” Why does that make the speaker “a happy fly” whether he lives or dies?
facilitatorNotes: If thinking is what makes life, then while he thinks he is alive and content, and dying does not take that away. The ending is a puzzle; readers can say what they make of it, and that puzzling over it is itself thinking.
evidence: If thought is life
A happy fly.

readings.title: The Angel (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Tell a dream in order, then ask the dreamer’s own question: “What can it mean?”
readings.focus: A dreamer hides her happiness and arms herself against kindness until it is too late.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. The speaker is telling a dream. A maiden Queen is a young, unmarried queen. “Witless woe was ne’er beguiled” is hard: witless means foolish, woe is sorrow, and beguiled means charmed away, so it means something like “foolish sorrow was never so fooled.”

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Angel,” the complete poem; opens “I dreamt a dream! What can it mean? And that I was a maiden Queen Guarded by an Angel…”; closes “…armed, he came in vain; For the time of youth was fled, And grey hairs were on my head.”.

questions.prompt: Who guards the dreamer, and what does the dreamer do day and night?
facilitatorNotes: A mild Angel guards her. She weeps day and night; he wipes her tears away; she hides her “heart’s delight” from him.
evidence: Guarded by an Angel mild:
And hid from him my heart’s delight.

questions.prompt: What happens after the Angel flies away?
facilitatorNotes: Morning comes, she dries her tears and “armed” her fears with ten thousand shields and spears. Instead of being sad, she gets ready to fight.
evidence: I dried my tears, and armed my fears
With ten thousand shields and spears.

questions.prompt: Why does the Angel come back “in vain”? Find two reasons in the last stanza.
facilitatorNotes: She is armed against him, and she has grown old: her youth has fled and her hair is grey. The chance has passed.
evidence: I was armed, he came in vain;
And grey hairs were on my head.

questions.prompt: The dreamer asks, “What can it mean?” What do you think she lost by hiding her delight and arming her fears?
facilitatorNotes: One reading: she kept away the kindness she was offered and the happiness of her young days, and only knew it when it was too late. Another: the Angel’s leaving taught her to protect herself. Readers can use the reversed lines “night and day” and “day and night” to show how long she wept.
evidence: I dreamt a dream! What can it mean?
For the time of youth was fled,

readings.title: The Tiger (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Hear a poem made almost entirely of questions, and notice the one word that changes at the end.
readings.focus: The speaker wonders who could make a creature so beautiful and so terrible.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. Symmetry is the matching of two sides, as in a face or a pair of stripes; sinews are strong cords that join muscle to bone; an anvil is the iron block a blacksmith hammers hot metal on.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Tiger,” the complete poem; opens “Tiger, tiger, burning bright In the forests of the night, What immortal hand or eye Could…”; closes “…In the forests of the night, What immortal hand or eye Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?”.

questions.prompt: Why might the tiger seem to be “burning bright” in a forest at night? What do you picture?
facilitatorNotes: Orange and black stripes like flames, glowing eyes, standing out against the dark trees. The fire returns later in “the fire of thine eyes.”
evidence: Tiger, tiger, burning bright
Burnt the fire of thine eyes?

questions.prompt: Stanza four is full of tools. What kind of work does the maker seem to be doing?
facilitatorNotes: A blacksmith’s work: hammer, chain, furnace and anvil. The tiger seems forged like hot iron, not born.
evidence: What the hammer? what the chain?
In what furnace was thy brain?

questions.prompt: Which question compares the tiger with another animal? Why is it a surprising question?
facilitatorNotes: “Did He who made the lamb make thee?” The lamb is gentle and the tiger fierce; could one maker have made both? Blake has a poem called “The Lamb” in Songs of Innocence.
evidence: Did He who made the lamb make thee?

questions.prompt: The first and last stanzas are almost the same, but “Could frame” becomes “Dare frame.” What difference does that one word make?
facilitatorNotes: “Could” asks who was able to make the tiger; “dare” asks who was brave enough. By the end, the speaker’s wonder has grown into something closer to fear. Some readers hear admiration in “dare” as well.
evidence: Could frame thy fearful symmetry?
Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?

readings.title: Three flower songs: My Pretty Rose Tree, Ah, Sunflower, and The Lily (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Read three short poems printed together and compare what each flower wants or does.
readings.focus: Flowers that feel like people: a jealous rose tree, a longing sunflower, a lily with no defences.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. These poems are from Songs of Experience. “Such a flower as May never bore” means a finer flower than any May ever grew; “passed … o’er” means passed it by. A sunflower turns its face to follow the sun across the sky; a clime is a land; “pined away with desire” means wasted away from wishing; aspire means rise up toward something.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “My Pretty Rose Tree,” “Ah, Sunflower,” and “The Lily,” the three complete poems; opens “A flower was offered to me, Such a flower as May never bore; But I said, ‘I’ve a pretty…”; closes “…the Lily white shall in love delight, Nor a thorn nor a threat stain her beauty bright.”.

questions.prompt: In “My Pretty Rose Tree,” why does the speaker turn down the beautiful flower? How does the rose tree repay him?
facilitatorNotes: He is loyal to the rose tree he already has. But the rose turns away “with jealousy,” and all he gets is her thorns. His loyalty is not rewarded.
evidence: But I said, ‘I’ve a pretty rose tree,’
But my rose turned away with jealousy,

questions.prompt: What does the sunflower do all day? Where does it want to go?
facilitatorNotes: It “countest the steps of the sun,” following it across the sky, and longs for the “sweet golden clime” where the traveller’s journey is done. Many readers take that place to be heaven, where even the dead “Arise from their graves.”
evidence: Who countest the steps of the sun;
Seeking after that sweet golden clime

questions.prompt: The rose has a thorn and the sheep has a horn. What does the Lily have instead?
facilitatorNotes: No thorn and no threat: she delights in love, and nothing stains her beauty. She is the only flower of the three with no way to hurt anyone.
evidence: The modest Rose puts forth a thorn,
Nor a thorn nor a threat stain her beauty bright.

questions.prompt: Choose one of the three poems. Is it only about a flower, or could it be about people too? Explain.
facilitatorNotes: The rose tree could be about jealousy between friends; the sunflower about longing to be somewhere better; the lily about loving without defending yourself. Some readers will prefer to keep them about flowers, which is fair too. The answer should rest on one line.
evidence: And her thorns were my only delight.
Where my Sunflower wishes to go!

readings.title: The Garden of Love (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Notice what has replaced each happy thing the speaker remembers.
readings.focus: A place of play becomes a place of rules and graves.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. A chapel is a small church. “Thou shalt not” is how most of the Ten Commandments begin in the old English Bible. Priests are church ministers; briars are thorny stems.
readings.contentNote: Blake criticises the strict churches of his time for forbidding joy. It is his view, and a sharp one; families may hold different views about church and rules.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Garden of Love,” the complete poem; opens “I went to the Garden of Love, And saw what I never had seen; A Chapel was built in the…”; closes “…in black gowns were walking their rounds, And binding with briars my joys and desires.”.

questions.prompt: What has been built in the place where the speaker used to play?
facilitatorNotes: A chapel, “in the midst,” right on the green where they played.
evidence: A Chapel was built in the midst,
Where I used to play on the green.

questions.prompt: What is written over the chapel door? What do the words and the shut gates tell you about this chapel?
facilitatorNotes: “Thou shalt not”: the start of a rule forbidding something. With the gates shut, the chapel seems to keep people out and tell them what not to do, rather than welcome them.
evidence: And the gates of this Chapel were shut,
And ‘Thou shalt not’ writ over the door;

questions.prompt: What does the speaker find in the garden instead of flowers?
facilitatorNotes: Graves and tombstones, and priests in black gowns walking their rounds. The garden that “so many sweet flowers bore” is now full of death.
evidence: And I saw it was filled with graves,
And tombstones where flowers should be;

questions.prompt: The last two lines are longer than the others and rhyme inside themselves (“gowns … rounds,” “briars … desires”). How does that sound fit what the priests are doing?
facilitatorNotes: The long lines drag on, and the inside rhymes tie them up, the way briars bind the speaker’s joys. Some readers hear the rhythm as the priests’ slow walking. Read the last line aloud to test it.
evidence: And priests in black gowns were walking their rounds,
And binding with briars my joys and desires.

readings.title: The Little Vagabond (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Hear a child’s argument and decide what Blake is saying through it.
readings.focus: A poor child asks why church cannot be as warm and kind as the alehouse.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. A vagabond is a wanderer without a home. An alehouse sold ale, a kind of beer, and had a fire. To regale is to treat or feast someone; a parson is a minister. “Bandy” children have bowed legs, a sign of too little good food; fasting is going without food; a birch is a bundle of twigs once used to beat children. Apparel means clothes.
readings.contentNote: The child speaker praises the alehouse, where people drink beer, over the cold church. Blake is mocking churches that were harsh to poor children; the poem mentions hunger and beating.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Little Vagabond,” the complete poem; opens “Dear mother, dear mother, the Church is cold; But the Alehouse is healthy, and pleasant,…”; closes “…quarrel with the Devil or the barrel, But kiss him, and give him both drink and apparel.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the child prefer the alehouse to the church?
facilitatorNotes: The church is cold; the alehouse is “healthy, and pleasant, and warm,” and there he is treated well. He is thinking of comfort and kindness, not of drink.
evidence: Dear mother, dear mother, the Church is cold;
Besides, I can tell where I am used well;

questions.prompt: What does the child think the church should do? What would happen then?
facilitatorNotes: Give them some ale and a pleasant fire. Then they would sing and pray all day and never wish to leave.
evidence: But, if at the Church they would give us some ale,
We’d sing and we’d pray all the livelong day,

questions.prompt: What would change for Dame Lurch’s children?
facilitatorNotes: They would no longer have bandy legs, go hungry, or be beaten with the birch. The line shows what poor children suffered.
evidence: Would not have bandy children, nor fasting, nor birch.

questions.prompt: At the end, God makes friends with the Devil and gives him drink and clothes. Is the child just being silly, or is Blake making a serious point in a child’s voice?
facilitatorNotes: Both can be argued. The child’s idea is funny, but Blake suggests that a loving God, “like a father,” would want his children warm and happy, not cold and punished. Some readers find the ending shocking; ask them which line goes too far, and why.
evidence: And God, like a father, rejoicing to see
But kiss him, and give him both drink and apparel.

readings.title: Infant Sorrow (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Imagine being born, told by the baby itself.
readings.focus: A newborn struggles against the world and then gives up and sulks.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. The speaker is a newborn baby. Piping means crying in a high voice; a fiend is a devil or demon. Swaddling bands were strips of cloth wrapped tightly round a baby.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “Infant Sorrow,” the complete poem; opens “My mother groaned, my father wept: Into the dangerous world I leapt, Helpless, naked,…”; closes “…my swaddling bands, Bound and weary, I thought best To sulk upon my mother’s breast.”.

questions.prompt: What happens in the first two lines? How do the parents feel?
facilitatorNotes: The baby is born: the mother groans in pain, the father weeps, and the baby leaps “Into the dangerous world.” The father may be weeping for joy, worry or both.
evidence: My mother groaned, my father wept:
Into the dangerous world I leapt,

questions.prompt: How does the baby describe itself?
facilitatorNotes: Helpless, naked, crying loudly, “Like a fiend hid in a cloud.” It is tiny and weak but also wild and noisy.
evidence: Helpless, naked, piping loud,
Like a fiend hid in a cloud.

questions.prompt: What does the baby struggle against, and what does it decide to do in the end?
facilitatorNotes: Its father’s hands and its swaddling bands. Tired and bound, it decides it is best “To sulk upon my mother’s breast.”
evidence: Striving against my swaddling bands,
To sulk upon my mother’s breast.

questions.prompt: Is this a sweet poem about a baby, like a lullaby? What does Blake show that lullabies leave out?
facilitatorNotes: Not really: the baby fights, sulks, and calls the world “dangerous.” Some readers find it funny and true to life; others find it sad that a baby must give up. Both views can use the words “struggling” and “sulk.”
evidence: Struggling in my father’s hands,
Bound and weary, I thought best

readings.title: A Poison Tree (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Follow a comparison that runs through a whole poem: anger grown like a plant.
readings.focus: Anger that is hidden instead of spoken grows into something deadly.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. Wrath is anger; a foe is an enemy; “deceitful wiles” are tricks; “when the night had veiled the pole” means when night had covered the sky.
readings.contentNote: The poem ends with the speaker glad to see his enemy lying under the tree, apparently killed by the poisoned apple.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “A Poison Tree,” the complete poem; opens “I was angry with my friend: I told my wrath, my wrath did end. I was angry with my foe: I…”; closes “…had veiled the pole; In the morning, glad, I see My foe outstretched beneath the tree.”.

questions.prompt: What happened when the speaker told his friend he was angry? What happened when he did not tell his foe?
facilitatorNotes: With the friend, the anger ended; with the foe, it grew. The whole poem grows from that difference.
evidence: I told my wrath, my wrath did end.
I told it not, my wrath did grow.

questions.prompt: The speaker grows his anger like a plant. What does he water it and give it sunshine with?
facilitatorNotes: He waters it with fears and tears and suns it with smiles and tricks: false friendliness that hides the anger.
evidence: And I watered it in fears
And I sunnèd it with smiles

questions.prompt: Why does the foe creep into the garden at night?
facilitatorNotes: He sees the bright apple and knows it belongs to the speaker; he wants it, perhaps out of envy or rivalry. The foe does wrong too: he steals.
evidence: And my foe beheld it shine,
And he knew that it was mine,—

questions.prompt: How does the speaker feel in the morning? What do you think Blake wants readers to notice about that?
facilitatorNotes: He is “glad.” The gladness is the most frightening part: hidden anger has turned him cruel. Many readers take the poem as a warning to speak about anger before it grows; others notice that both men chose badly.
evidence: In the morning, glad, I see
My foe outstretched beneath the tree.

readings.title: A Divine Image (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Find the pattern of four in each stanza and read the poem as an answer to another poem.
readings.focus: People can carry cruelty and fear as easily as kindness.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. In Songs of Innocence, Blake’s poem “The Divine Image” says that Mercy has a human heart, Pity a human face, Love “the human form divine,” and Peace the human dress. This poem answers it. Divine means godlike. A forge is a blacksmith’s fire for shaping iron; a furnace is a closed oven of great heat; a gorge here is a greedy throat.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “A Divine Image,” the complete poem; opens “Cruelty has a human heart, And Jealousy a human face; Terror the human form divine, And…”; closes “…form a fiery forge, The human face a furnace sealed, The human heart its hungry gorge.”.

questions.prompt: Which four unkind feelings does the first stanza give to the human heart, face, form and dress?
facilitatorNotes: Cruelty, Jealousy, Terror and Secrecy. Each is matched to one part of a person.
evidence: Cruelty has a human heart,
And Secrecy the human dress.

questions.prompt: In the second stanza, what are the dress, form, face and heart turned into?
facilitatorNotes: Forged iron, a fiery forge, a sealed furnace and a hungry gorge. The person becomes something hard, hot, shut and greedy.
evidence: The human dress is forgèd iron,
The human heart its hungry gorge.

questions.prompt: Why might Blake pick iron, a forge and a furnace for these pictures?
facilitatorNotes: They are hard, burning and closed: you cannot see inside a sealed furnace, just as Secrecy hides. Blake was also a craftsman who worked with metal plates, so a workshop was familiar to him. Readers may have other reasons.
evidence: The human form a fiery forge,
The human face a furnace sealed,

questions.prompt: The Innocence poem says Mercy has a human heart; this one says Cruelty does. Can both be true?
facilitatorNotes: Many readers say yes: people can be merciful or cruel, and Blake shows both sides. Others may think one poem is truer. Ask for an example from a story or from life, without naming real people unkindly.
evidence: Cruelty has a human heart,

readings.title: A Cradle Song (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Hear a lullaby that is both tender and worried.
readings.focus: A parent watches a sleeping baby and wonders what the waking world will bring.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. Songs of Innocence has a cradle song too; this one is the Experience song. Wiles are tricks, and cunning means sly or clever at tricks. To trace is to make out something faint.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “A Cradle Song,” the complete poem; opens “Sleep, sleep, beauty bright, Dreaming in the joys of night; Sleep, sleep; in thy sleep…”; closes “…heart asleep! When thy little heart doth wake, Then the dreadful light shall break.”.

questions.prompt: What does the singer see in the sleeping baby’s face?
facilitatorNotes: Soft desires, secret joys, secret smiles, and “pretty infant wiles.” The singer watches very closely.
evidence: Soft desires I can trace,
Secret joys and secret smiles,

questions.prompt: Even while the baby sleeps, what “sit and weep”?
facilitatorNotes: “Little sorrows.” Even a sleeping baby is not completely free of sadness.
evidence: Little sorrows sit and weep.

questions.prompt: What does the singer think will happen when the baby’s heart wakes?
facilitatorNotes: “Then the dreadful light shall break.” One reading: the baby will meet the troubles of the world; another: the baby’s own cunning tricks will show. Either way, waking is not entirely happy.
evidence: When thy little heart doth wake,
Then the dreadful light shall break.

questions.prompt: Is this a comforting lullaby? Sort its words into soft ones and worrying ones.
facilitatorNotes: Soft: sleep, sweet, smiles, softest. Worrying: sorrows, cunning, creep, dreadful. The mix makes it tender and uneasy at once. Some readers hear love most strongly; others hear fear.
evidence: Sleep, sleep, beauty bright,
O the cunning wiles that creep

readings.title: The Schoolboy (Songs of Experience)
readings.challenge: Follow a comparison from a bird to a child to a growing plant.
readings.focus: A boy argues that a child kept from joy cannot grow well.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. Schools in Blake’s time were often strict places where children sat silent for hours. A huntsman “winds his horn” by blowing it; a bower is a shady shelter of leaves; drooping means hanging down, tired and sad.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Schoolboy,” the complete poem; opens “I love to rise in a summer morn, When the birds sing on every tree; The distant huntsman…”; closes “…what griefs destroy, Or bless the mellowing year, When the blasts of winter appear?”.

questions.prompt: What does the boy love about a summer morning? Find the sounds he hears.
facilitatorNotes: Birds singing on every tree, a huntsman’s horn far off, and a skylark that sings “with me.” He calls them “sweet company.”
evidence: When the birds sing on every tree;
And the skylark sings with me:

questions.prompt: What happens to his joy at school? Which words describe the teacher?
facilitatorNotes: School “drives all joy away”; the teacher is only “a cruel eye outworn,” a tired and unkind eye always watching.
evidence: O it drives all joy away!
Under a cruel eye outworn,

questions.prompt: Stanza four compares a child to a bird. What is the cage?
facilitatorNotes: School, or any place that keeps a child from joy. A bird born for joy cannot sing in a cage.
evidence: How can the bird that is born for joy
Sit in a cage and sing?

questions.prompt: In the last two stanzas the boy talks to his parents about buds, blossoms and summer fruit. What is he warning them about?
facilitatorNotes: If a child’s joy is “nipped” like a bud, the child will not grow well, and the “summer” of later life will not come in joy. Some readers think he exaggerates and that school matters; ask which lines make his case strongest.
evidence: O father and mother if buds are nipped,
How shall the summer arise in joy,

readings.title: The Voice of the Ancient Bard (Songs of Experience)
readings.workTitle: The Voice of the Ancient Bard
readings.challenge: Follow a speaker who calls the young to look at a new morning and warns them about a maze.
readings.focus: An old poet invites young people to see truth fresh, away from quarrels and folly.
readings.context: William Blake (1757–1827) was a London poet and painter who printed his own books, etching each poem and its pictures onto copper and coloring the pages by hand. Songs of Innocence (1789) and Songs of Experience (1794) often answer each other: the same subject seen first with trusting eyes, then with troubled ones. This poem is from Songs of Experience. It is the last poem in the book. A bard is a poet-singer of long ago. The opening morn is the dawn. Disputes are arguments; “artful teazing” (an old spelling of teasing) means clever, tiresome arguing. Folly is foolishness; to perplex is to confuse.

excerpt.locator: Songs of Experience, “The Voice of the Ancient Bard,” the complete poem; opens “Youth of delight! come hither And see the opening morn, Image of Truth new-born. Doubt is…”; closes “…And feel—they know not what but care; And wish to lead others, when they should be led.”.

questions.prompt: Whom does the Bard call, and what does he ask them to see?
facilitatorNotes: The “Youth of delight,” young people, to come and see the opening morning, which he calls the “Image of Truth new-born.”
evidence: Youth of delight! come hither
Image of Truth new-born.

questions.prompt: What does the Bard say has gone away?
facilitatorNotes: Doubt, “clouds of reason,” dark disputes and artful teasing. The morning clears away arguing as well as darkness.
evidence: Doubt is fled, and clouds of reason,
Dark disputes and artful teazing.

questions.prompt: How does the Bard describe Folly? What happens to people who go there?
facilitatorNotes: Folly is an endless maze with tangled roots. Many have fallen; they stumble all night over the bones of the dead and feel only worry.
evidence: Folly is an endless maze;
They stumble all night over bones of the dead;

questions.prompt: The poem ends: people “wish to lead others, when they should be led.” What do you think the Bard means? Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: Those lost in folly try to tell others the way, though they are lost themselves. Some readers think the Bard means they should follow the truth of the new morning; others that the old should sometimes listen to the young. Ask for a time when someone led who should have listened.
evidence: And wish to lead others, when they should be led.
